source_text: Deinde post dies paucos Pudens miles optio, praepositus carceris, nos magnificare coepit intellegens magnam uirtutem esse in nobis; qui multos ad nos admittebat, ut et nos et illi inuicem refrigeraremus. Ut autem proximauit dies muneris, intrat ad me pater meus consumptus taedio, et coepit barbam suam euellere et in terram mittere, et prosternere se in faciem, et inproperare annis suis et dicere tanta uerba quae mouerent uniuersam creaturam. Ego dolebam pro infelici senecta eius.
pass_a_gloss: Then after a few days Pudens, a soldier, an optio, the warden of the prison, began to esteem us highly, perceiving that great strength was in us; he kept letting many people in to see us, so that we and they might in turn get relief from one another. When the day of the public spectacle drew close, my father came in to me worn down by distress, and began to tear out his beard and throw it to the ground, and to cast himself down on his face, and to reproach his years and to say such words as would move the whole creation. I was pained for his miserable old age.
pass_b_english: Then, after a few days, Pudens, a soldier and optio who was in charge of the prison, began to honor us, for he perceived that a great strength was in us; he admitted many visitors to us, so that we and they might find relief in one another.

But as the day of the games drew near, my father came in to me, consumed with grief, and he began to pluck out his beard and cast it to the ground, and to throw himself down on his face, and to reproach his own years and to speak words so piteous that they would have moved the whole creation. I grieved for his unhappy old age.

lemmas.gloss: junior officer, aide to a centurion
officer in charge of the prison
to honor, hold in high regard

choices.why: with dies proximauit it denotes the scheduled gladiatorial munus, not a gift in general
subjunctive of purpose after ut, reciprocal inuicem, for respite in prison rather than literal cooling
